utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning. Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Oric, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow the proceedings in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will repeat the question just in case there is something wrong going on with the interpretation. Mechanical I would imagine. It's okay. Can you follow -- can you hear me in the first place and can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. I can follow and I hear you well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a chair. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Jan Wubben senior trial attorney together with co-counsel Ms. Patricia Sellers, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and case manager Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and your team. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with my colleague John Jones I am Defence counsel for Naser Oric. Our case manager Mr. Geoff Roberts is with us and Miss Jasmina Cosic our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Before we proceed with the normal business that we have on our agenda, this morning at about 8.00 or whatever time it was I came to my Chambers only to find my secretary, my assistant and the assistant of Judge Eser and Judge Brydensholt already there trying to sort out all the documents that were indicated as needed for today's sitting. And they were complaining, very rightly so I must say, because the list of the documents that were needed for this morning's sittings was only handed to them after 5.50 last Friday. Fortunately I have not had to deal with such inconveniences more than twice or three times in the last three years. So I have every reason to believe this will not happen again. But please do try when it's a weekend approaching that the list indicating the documents, the documents, if I said witnesses before I correct myself, I don't know what I did, but the list indicating the documents be given in good time to our staff otherwise they will either have to stay here overtime, or else, like happened over the weekend, come here before everyone else on a Monday morning to sort out the problem. I hope it will not repeat itself and I'm sure you will deal your utmost. At the moment we are dealing with the Prosecution case. Later on the same thing will be applied to the Defence when they come to their case. But this, the list of the documents, I take it, was handed to them after 5.30 on Friday. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I duly apply for any inconvenience caused. I took it as information that it was handed over earlier and I take it that it was at that time and, if so, we will try to do our best at the utmost that this will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you will. I don't doubt it in the least for a moment, but please make sure that you will. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm not sure we have the documents you referred to which are for today's sitting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't really -- received the list myself, it never comes to us. What usually happens, Mr. Jones, is the -- our staff receives a list like this which basically says: Trial number P whatever and then the ERN number and then the description of the exhibit. For example, the first one is P100, decisions of the staff of Srebrenica, armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We haven't received that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's even worse. That's even worse because you should be prepared well before, that is in good time, to know which documents the witness is going to be examined upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We had to go through a very elaborate process of locating through ERN numbers, documents, printing off them ourselves to try and understand how the reports will be presented today. If I may touch on another matter, although perhaps we should come to it later but you will also-- seen our urgent motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but we talked -- let's stick to this first. Is Mr. Jones correct in saying that he did not receive a similar document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution team believes that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Perhaps before you speak you can verify this. The information that I am getting now that usually it is sent to the e-mail address of the case manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So perhaps you can check. I mean in the other -- all the other cases that I have been dealing with, this problem has never arisen. So I don't see why it should arise in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, well our case manager and CaseMap manager informed me that they checked their e-mail at the weekend and they hadn't received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the same time as Chambers and the registrar in my administration -- verification of the case manager we sent it to their case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have the problem of the case manager saying that he has not received them, which puts me on the defensive because I don't know what to say. In anything, if necessary, and if you think you ought to -- you need the time, I will let you have a copy of this, Mr. Jones, or the registrar will and give you sufficient time to identify these documents and to have them ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We are -- as I say, we did go through an exercise of printing off the documents so we are ready nonetheless. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you require time we will give you time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Our manager will check his e-mail at the break and see if he received it. We checked at the weekend and it's not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the past I have had complaints from the Defence of this arriving at the eleventh hour, not allowing much time, et cetera, but not that it was not received. So please check into this and let's hope these are just teething troubles that we are having in this case as we try to start. I say as we try to start because last Friday then after 5.30 or whatever time it was, I don't remember what time it was, I was informed by my legal officer that she had been informed in turn by the Prosecution, by Ms. Sellers in particular, that the Prosecution had decided to withdraw Professor Gow from the list of witnesses. This was soon followed by another phone call informing me that the Defence had filed an urgent motion, which we will be returning very, very, very soon. In any case, we decided to postpone the matter until this morning and we will discuss it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm on my feet, Your Honour, because it's our motion and I can elaborate on the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you speak on your motion, however, I just want to make it clear that we did not view very positively the idea of withdrawing a witness, an important witness, two days before he is supposed to give evidence. Particularly taking into consideration the fact that as expected, him being an important witness, the Defence must have spent hours reading that report and preparing for the cross-examination, a statement which they confirm in the urgent motion. I have come across this in my life before as a Judge, as you can imagine it has happened before. I am not going to ask you why you have decided to withdraw your witness because it's within your right to decide who to call and who not to call. Certainly you should have given the matter more consideration and definitely not at the time which is very proximate to the day when this person was supposed to be giving evidence. It's lack of consideration in regard to the Defence and lack of consideration in regard to the Trial Chamber that does its utmost to make the best use of the time that we have available. It's very easy for you to come forward and say, yes, but on Wednesday don't worry, Judges, we will bring Ms. Manas. But we were on the pretext that what I heard Mr. Jones say in open court last week that he was -- they needed three days to cross-examine this witness, we were anticipating that the whole week or the rest of the week, starting from Wednesday onwards, will be dedicated to Professor Gow and possibly even Monday, the first day of next week, like this, it's a complete disruption of the whole programme. I mean, I can't look straight in the eyes of Madam Vidovic or Mr. Jones and say: Be patient. Don't worry. Wednesday we'll hear Manas and it's not a big problem because she is not the kind of witness that calls for a lot of preparation on the part of the Defence. But if you intend also to bring forward other witnesses who have given statements that the Defence have got to read, et cetera, that is lack of consideration, lack of consideration. So the very first thing I am going to do is to appeal to your good selves and to possibly reconsider your decision to withdraw Professor Gow. I know you are entitled to withdraw Professor Gow because it is in your rights, that much I know. But I also know that the consequence of this is that you will leave out of your case, out of your case the only expert evidence that you tended to bring forward as to the existence of a conflict, character of a conflict and the historical and political background leading to the events that we talk about in this case. It's true that that gap can be filled by the Defence, it's true that that gap can be filled by the Trial Chamber itself. But my suggestion and my exhortation to you is to take time and reconsider your decision. I would have nothing against postponing the evidence of Professor Gow from now until later. I have absolutely nothing, even though this may cause annoyance and inconvenience to the Defence. But I have no objection to that, but I do seriously and the three of us are in agreement on this. We look with concern. I mean, it's -- we are very unhappy with the fact that you have taken your decision when you have taken it and the way you have taken it. Of course you are entitled to take that decision. Yes, who is going to react? You, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Well, please be informed that we immediately as a first reaction informed Defence counsel by telephone and then wrote them a letter to confirm it and also Chambers to confirm on Friday. And that was right after the decision-making. When it comes to giving consideration, we tried to give it consideration and we took the decision in line of the developments within our own strategy, the indictment, the changes and from the beginning on our approach and also referring to our opening statement. That means, however, that the point is and the request is well-taken. And I will get back to you, if you allow me, Your Honour, after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and we will discuss the motion after the break then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, may I add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. If it's the case, remark. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly, Mr. Wubben said that they immediately informed the Defence. As you have seen in our motion we received a phone call at 5 to 5.00 on Friday afternoon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones it would have infuriated me if I were in your shoes. It would have infuriated me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's one point obviously, and the inconvenience. But there's another point and that's why I make it now which is to do with truth and reconciliation which Your Honours referred to. Your Honours referred to the importance of the trial as a discovery of the truth and the importance of these trials to achieve reconciliation in the region. And we just wonder what message it sends about discovery of the truth that the Prosecution want to drop the one witness who could start this trial by giving a complete picture of the political, historical, military background and instead they want to start with a labourer, I believe it is, from a town called Jezestica, which Your Honours won't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's their choice. I -- as you know, Mr. Jones, this is an adversarial system predominantly or preeminently an adversarial system and the Trial Chamber interferes as little as it can or tries not to interfere at all with the way each party decides to present its case. But on the other hand there are ways and means and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. I make that point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try to start the concept of having trials being conducted by means of surprises and hidden cards et cetera is long gone. It's finished. That was the last century, or the beginning of this century. Nowadays it's no longer like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's our concern, the tactics that are being used, tactics allowing us to waste time on the witness when the Prosecution in all possibility knew they were going to drop the witness. And in that regard I was wondering if Your Honours received the report of Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, we received-- that is another matter that obviously we will deal with. I understand. I haven't seen it but I understand that the report of Dr. Gow was amongst the documents that were tendered in the last sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If Your Honours didn't receive it, I would indicate an earlier decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if we have received it or not, to be honest with you. But in any case if this witness is going to be withdrawn, that document will also be sent back to the Prosecution because we will not keep it in our file unless we decide otherwise. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. I'll reserve my remarks to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we ought to discuss that for the time being. I still am hopeful that the good sense of the Prosecution will prevail. I mean it's too late in the day to withdraw such an important witness. The end result is we may have to call one ourselves, end result is you may have to call one yourselves. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as I stated, I get back to the Bench after the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Let me first protest against the insinuations by Mr. Jones with all respect to this counsel. Using the word like "tactics", it isn't right. I pointed out the change of the indictment in my opening statement, and if you look at the indictment from -- the past indictment from July 2003 and the latest indictment from last week, you will notice the difference, and you have of course -- but also that might change the nature and volume of the testimony given. So these are important changes and there is no way of tactics or abuse. And the tone of it, I'm really disappointed. That's not constructive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have to respond to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I think we can leave it at that, Mr. Jones. Come on, let's not create a chain of incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's simply that this is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Leave it, Mr. Jones, leave it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's simply in -- the indictment was amended two weeks ago. The Prosecution has had two weeks to consider that and they still had Dr. Gow on the list, so that's not an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The -- incidentally I'm informed by my LO that the Gow report was filed. I don't know about it because it was filed when the case was not yet assigned to this Trial Chamber. So it was filed with Trial Chamber III which was then presided by Judge Robinson. However, I can assure you that none of us have read this expert report and I actually thought it was much bigger than this. But anyway, it's -- I'm being -- yes ... So we'll come to this later and, Prosecution, try to heed our advice. First witness is Professor -- is it professor or Dr.? Doctorandus W.F.P. Fagel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he is Doctorandus. That's a kind of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How should I address him? How should I address? Dr.?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Doctorandus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Doctorandus?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Doctorandus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Doctorandus.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we start with the witness is it possible at this very moment to tender the declarations of -- and attachments of Stephen Tedder and Barney Kelly has announced already and accepted by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection on your part, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Please call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, I suppose the witness is English-speaking, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, he is English-speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence in this case, instituted by the Prosecution against Naser Oric. And our rules require that before you do so you enter a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Our usher will hand you the solemn declaration. Please read it out loud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat. You are first going to be asked a series of questions that we refer to as the examination-in-chief by Mr. Wubben. He will ask you to tell us who you are and what your qualifications and experience are and then the reason for your presence here and the rest of the information that will be asked from you. And then later on you will be cross-examined by -- who is going to cross-examine --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I will be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- by Mr. Jones on behalf of the Defence team. Yes, Mr. Wubben, he is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Witness, may I have your name, please?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: My name is Wilhelmus Petrus Franciscus Fagel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And what's your age?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Age is 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And what's your occupation?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: I am a forensic handwriting examiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You are a forensic -- in an institute?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: I am working for the Netherlands Forensics Institute in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that in a laboratory?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: The Netherlands Forensic Institute is part of the Dutch Ministry of Justice as a relatively autonomous service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And I take it that it is independent more or less?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes. We are not a police laboratory and it's not part of the Prosecution division.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: How long are you employed as such?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: 21 years and a couple of months more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What are your present duties?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: I'm still working as a handwriting examiner full time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Tell me about your formal education.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: I have studied psychology at the University of Amsterdam and specialised in psycholinguistics, and graduated with a subsidiary in general linguistics in 1978. Then I've been working for a few years for the University of Amsterdam before I joined the Netherlands Forensic Institute in 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What other training do you have related to this job?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: I got my training fully at the Netherlands Forensic Institute by so-called training on the job and literature studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you or are you a member of an international network of colleagues, forensic experts?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: I'm a member of a European organisation called GFS which stands for Gesselschaft fuer Forensische Schrift, schrift [sic] expertise and I am also a member of the steering committee of the European network of forensic handwriting examiners. Actually, I'm at the moment the chairman of this steering committee. This is one of the expert working groups of the European Network Forensic Science Institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Is this part of a kind of network also of institutes for laboratories?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: It's a network, an organisation of police and government forensic institutes in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And how do you maintain or do you know the quality of your work, is that also shared or not?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes, we have regular meetings where we try to describe or harmonise our methods among other things and exchange other information. If we have some special cases we might show it to other people and we organise conferences, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Is this just a few countries who have to cooperate on this or is it more --

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Most European countries have one or more institutes which are part of this organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you publish also articles or books or whatsoever from your profession?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Can you tell me something about it.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Well, before I joined the Netherlands Forensic Institute, I published some articles on forensic -- not on forensic, but on speaker identification, et cetera, but it's not very relevant, so I will limit myself to the relevant articles on handwriting examination. Well, I think I published some -- among others an article on the method -- our method, methodological aspects of handwriting identification in the Journal of Document Examination and, well, a few other articles. I don't know if you want me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, no thank you, but is it throughout the years or only recent or ...

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: I think I published the first article in 1986 and, well, it's about -- the last one in 2003. It's, I think, about one article a year, maybe some more, maybe some less.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: How many handwriting examinations do you apply in a given year?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: On the average I've done about 100 examinations in a year in the last 21 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Can you give as an estimation of the total number?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Must be more than 2.000, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Do you make such analysis as a regular part of your duties?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you ever testify in a Tribunal or in court before?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: I did, but only in Dutch court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I need some guidance by the Trial Chamber. I intended to request if you accept the qualifications as an expert, but I also recall that you have a specific policy on dealing with matters like that. So if it is not now the appropriate time but further later on in this trial, then I will postpone that request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have anything to say from Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We didn't challenge the qualifications of the expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think so. It's not my recollection that you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, I didn't do so, but it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. It's -- the Defence did not challenge the qualifications of your expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So there is a moment when I showed to you through this witness his background, his training, allocation, his work, how long he worked, that whenever the Defence do not challenge the expert witness's qualifications, I would like to request this Trial Chamber to accept his qualifications as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The way we go about it is you still have the onus of proving that he is an expert. Now, how you prove it is your business. If you can prove it by his own testimony, if you can prove it by a proper CV confirmed by him in evidence, or during his evidence. It's up to you. And then it's up to us to decide whether that evidence is enough to qualify him as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we obviously will take it into consideration the fact that his qualifications are not being contested by the Defence. The fact that you in your good judgement chose him as your expert, the renown of the Netherlands Forensic Institute, which is no joke. I mean, it's -- we are not dealing with an institute that is embarking on forensic expertise. We are dealing with a very experienced institute. We will take everything into consideration. But I cannot tell you here and now, yes, we are happy with the qualifications of your expert. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, you have answered my question. I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the first time I have seen him in my life, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: This is not the time to put the qualifications --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I will proceed with my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Please, witness, will you give the Judges a short introductions of the phases in comparative handwriting examinations in general as practiced by this forensic institute and adopted by you.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try. The method I -- that is used by the -- in the Netherlands Forensic Institute is explained in annex 1 to the report. This method is accredited by the Dutch accreditation board with its associated systems of quality assurance. Basically, it -- in a comparative handwriting examination there are four stages, these include handwriting analysis, analysis of the features of the handwriting, comparison of the similarities and differences -- sorry, comparison of the observed handwriting characteristics, then the assessment of the similarities and differences found. And finally, drawing the conclusion. Now, each of these stages can be broken down in more phases. I'm not sure whether you want me to go into that amount of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: As a kind of introduction, general introduction, it will be helpful to assist the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Well, the method of the Netherlands Forensic Institute distinguishes the main categories of handwriting characteristics, the general or overall characteristics, which include things like -- I mean, this is not only for signatures but handwriting in general, this includes the style of writing, the size of the handwriting, the slope of the writing, the degrees of -- the degree of connectivity, the pressure variation, et cetera. Then we have the surface layout characteristics, the width of the left and right margins, the distance between words and lines, but these are more -- apply more to written text than to signatures. And finally, most important, what we call the microcharacteristics. These are the shape, the proportions of the -- the visual element, the segmental parts of the handwriting, in most cases the letters and numbers and other characteristics. These are all -- each of these characteristics in the writing is evaluated and then compared, after which we -- based on these similarities or differences that we found we draw a conclusion as to the probability that a handwriting -- a questioned handwriting has been written by the person who gave the sample -- the known writing, the reference samples. And each handwriting examination is done by two examiners in our lab and they draw their conclusion independently and then it is compared to each other and it's -- according to our methods, both examiners must reach a unanimous conclusion. Is this enough for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. Will you please address the -- more about the issue of the comparison and the weighing when it comes to the factors of similarities and the outcome of it, including the dissimilarities.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Well, as I said, most important are the microcharacteristics, the shape and proportions and individual elements within the handwriting or the signature. These are compared to each other. We try to -- when we compare them, we use the principle of visual equivalence. It's -- it takes too much time to really measure all the -- quantify all the characteristics that we -- that we evaluate. So we do it by -- actually breaking down the handwriting into separate elements, compare each of the elements. And if it fits into the variations within the reference material, we judge it as a similarity. And the more it fits, the better the similarity could -- the better the quality of the similarity. If it's a difference -- if they are not the same, then we say it is a dissimilarity or a difference. So for each of all the -- each of the elements we have partial evaluation of its similarity or difference and then we look at the overall results and base our conclusion on whether the handwriting has been written by the same person or not. And some of the -- especially when it's written elements, some of the elements, some of the shape forms, construction of letters may be more rare than others so these have a larger weight in our evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Can you clarify more about the finalisation, meaning drawing the conclusions and the probability scale.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Yeah. The results of a comparative handwriting examination can be presented in the form of a conclusion indicating to what extent the examiner considers it likely that the questioned writing was produced by the writer of the known samples, and this can be done on a scale which is a continuum between the writing was definitely written by this person and the writing was definitely not written by this person. But at the Netherlands Forensic Institute, we don't give categorical opinions, no certainty opinions, instead we use the wording -- the questioned writing was or was produced by the writer of the note samples with probability reaching on certainty. This is our strongest opinion. So at the positive side as well as at the negative side. The number of intermediary steps is rather arbitrary. The Netherlands Forensic Institute now uses highly probable -- probably -- probably not -- highly probable not as steps with inconsistent or, as we say, no opinion in between, in between the positive and negative conclusions. In some cases where we have problem applying one of these wordings, you may use the wordings possibly written by, or we might even say that the results of the examination do not support the proposition that the questioned signature was written by the person in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: When can one say that, for example -- you might give an example there is a kind of 100 per cent certainty?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: When there is enough writing and it's written fluently and we find very good similarities between the questioned writing and the reference samples, then we might say that the writing is written by this person with probability reaching on certainty. So this will be -- might be with about two or three lines of written text or a signature which is complicated enough to be difficult to copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And highly probably?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Highly probably, highly probably in that -- well, it's less than probable -- that may be because there are -- if in case of signatures because a signature is not that complex that a very good forger might be able to copy the signature in such a way that it's hard to distinguish from a real signature, but it's still very unprobable, highly unprobably that it can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I would like to proceed with the signatures. There are, I guess, various signatures possible. Do you make a distinction also in genuine signatures or imitations or pictures or forgery. What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: The signatures, there are various possibilities. A signature may be written by the owner and can be in his normal signature. And a signature can also be made by -- in the owner's name by someone else, so in that case it may be a forgery. But even we discern so-called bona fide - I don't know the English pronunciation - bona fide and mala fide signatures. A bona fide signature is, for example, a genuine signature written by the owner which does note deviate from its overall design. There are no signs of copying. It might be also -- the owner might have another signature, used another signature which deviates from the overall design which doesn't show any copying. So this is not a signature which has been written for -- to fool someone but it's just another signature someone uses. And the mala fide signatures, we have four types. This might be a clear -- a normal imitation of someone's signature which does not deviate in overall design but normally it shows signs of copying. It might be a pseudo-imitation signature. The owner of the signature might try to produce a signature which looks like an imitation, so he might even trace his own signature. Then there's a fictitious signature if someone wants to make a signature for a person but he doesn't know how this signature looks like, he can just make a fantasy signature in the name of this person. And then there may also be a pseudo-fictitious signature, for example, if I don't -- I want to -- I have to make -- put down a signature somewhere and later I want to say, well, that's not my signature. I might -- might just produce some kind of -- of doodle or some signature which doesn't look like my normal signature at all. These are the several kinds of possibilities we distinguish.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. The validation or conclusion. Is there any validation? Can you tell us about this issue.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: In the first place, as I told before, the method is accredited by the Dutch accreditation board, a board with an associated system of quality assurance. Secondly, as I also said, each comparative handwriting examination according to our method must be checked by a second examiner and both examiners must reach a unanimous conclusion. And finally the handwriting examiners of the Netherlands Forensics Institute are participating in European, American, and Australian proficiency tests, so-called collaborative exercises or skill validation trials.

And I quote: "At all times, new paragraph 20, relevant to this indictment a state of armed conflict existed on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Well, Your Honour, it is a principle that the Prosecution calls and decides upon the witnesses. When it comes to an important and dramatic change like that, and we first intend to call Gow for five and a half hours to establish that first prior paragraph of the indictment with the important elements of then-international character or armed conflict, apart from the armed conflict itself as a nucleus. So it is the Prosecution's opinion that the principle is and remains that we will call and decide upon our witnesses to establish such a paragraph within our indictment. That can be done through an expert, through witnesses. Already you will have noticed that the expert report was around -- it was limited in size around 10 -- 11, 12 pages as I recall. And after having deciding on the indictment by this Trial Chamber, we have to also reconsider for ourselves in an expeditious trial to be in such a way that we are able to prove our case with the witnesses provided. Thus, we didn't take a decision just like that. It was a shared decision by senior management and we took that decision. I know that I don't have to clarify or confirm this because tactics are the matter of the party that brings the witnesses forward. But I noticed also -- and that point was well-taken, that this Trial Chamber needs this witness or might need this witness for their own purposes. And I know about the powers of this Trial Chamber, proprio motu. But with a view to your open information, to your words, the Prosecution team, we are ready to reconsider our opinion in that regard and to accommodate this Trial Chamber to facilitate this Trial Chamber upon this information shared with us this morning. We contacted Victims and Witnesses Unit. We learned from -- over the weekend that --

utterances.text: From who? Over the weekend. I just moved the headphones for a second and I missed those words and thought you mentioned the name of someone.

Please accept this clarification of tactics out of respect for your Trial Chamber to show that whatever has been argued by the Defence counsel is really not true and can be clarified and justified by the argumentations I put forward. And I know and I hope that this Trial Chamber still confirms the opinion that it is up to the party to call and decide upon their witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben. I don't need you, Mr. Jones, to -- or Madam Vidovic to proceed with this matter any further. I think on behalf of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser and of course on my own behalf I wish to thank you and the other members of your team and anybody else from the Office of the Prosecution you may have consulted for your cooperation. Of course - and I make it very clear here - that we recognise the right of each party to decide which witnesses to bring forward and which witnesses not to bring forward. But I can imagine what it would be like if Madam Vidovic hands us the list of the witnesses they intend to bring forward later on in their case and then, as happened in many other cases, they decide not to bring forward some of their witnesses, including expert witnesses, I can imagine what the reaction would be if you stood up and said, no, but we insist that that witness be brought over by the Trial Chamber itself or you tried to bring that witness because the Defence is not bringing it. So let's make it very clear on our part. On our part we do of course recognise the principle in the adversarial system that -- which is the system that this Tribunal preeminently has adopted on which every party is able to decide which witnesses to bring forward and which witnesses not to bring forward with the caveat of course of matters, for example, related to relevance and other things. But now that the incident is practically over. The other, I wish you to understand why we put our foot in this and tried to put some pressure -- bring some pressure to bear. In reality you heard Mr. Jones or Madam Vidovic last week say in response to a remark that I myself made relating to the expert report of Mr. Gow, I had not read the expert report of Mr. Gow. I mean, I do not take it a habit of reading the entire case before it starts, the fact -- what I can avoid reading I avoid reading actually. But I was informed by members of my staff that had read the report after it was presented on the 6th of September to the previous Trial Chamber that much of it related to the internationality character of the armed conflict. And I did highlight that to you in all fairness to you to consider the time we require when handling this -- the testimony of this document -- of this expert. Certainly it was not my intention to give you a hint, now we don't need him, drop him. Definitely it was not my intention, especially after Mr. Jones stood up and said: Yes, Your Honour, it's true that -- but precisely we contend that for some of the charges, counts, that we have, even with the amendments, you still require the element of internationality of the conflict. Whether he is right or not, that doesn't matter. We are not going to deal with that. But his suggestion was that he would certainly need adequate time to cross-examine this witness on precisely the matter of cross-examination. Obviously we have submissions on whether the internationality of the conflict is relevant or not, but these are pleasures yet to come, and I do not intend to address them now, for sure. Which would have meant that had you stuck to your decision to drop this witness, expert witness, you would have put either us in a situation where we ourselves would have had to call an expert witness to deal with these aspects. This would have involved this Tribunal in unnecessary extra expenses which need not be covered now. This is why we are indeed grateful for the practical and pragmatic approach that you are taking. And depending on the issue, if there is no expert witness on your part and until and unless we produce an expert witness ourselves, then the ball will be in the Defence's court to see whether they need to bring forward a witness themselves. But from past experience, I can tell you that that takes time, it takes time even to locate a witness, an expert witness, and to get him agreed to the terms that usually this Tribunal offers. So you have done the Trial Chamber a great favour today and we do indeed want to show our appreciation for it. But for the future, if there is any witness that either you or later on the Defence you intend to drop, please give adequate prior notice to the other party and to the Trial Chamber, because sometimes I get my staff working on this and on that in anticipation of next week's sitting. And I'm sure that the Defence will not be sleeping in between one week and another in anticipation of the witnesses that you intend to produce. So try to make it the pattern and the rule for the future in the course of this trial that any changes, either in the names of witnesses you intend to bring forward or the order in which you intend to bring them forward or dropping of any witnesses you give prior notice of -- to the other party. It's not a question of tactics only; part of it is tactics and I acknowledge that you can resort to tactics. When I was Defence counsel myself I used to resort to tactics. But there is a limit, there is a limit, because over here it is a different kind of trial than what you get in the domestic jurisdiction. Here you have a lot of personnel working, photocopying, working, preparing notes for us, summaries. Defence is obviously reading in preparation of the witnesses to come, preparing cross-examination. So let's try to avoid all this confusion because these are matters that hurt and when they hurt they provoke a reaction. So once more, thank you, Mr. Wubben. And you will let us know what the situation is as we go along. In the meantime what is important if he doesn't come -- doesn't show up on Thursday -- Wednesday, then you get Manas.

For all the other signatures which were only available in a copy -- in quite a poor copy, I could only conclude that they were the same as with respect to the general design. So all I can say about these signatures is they are possibly written by this person, except for the signature Q6 which has a different design. But again, this signature is rather -- has a rather poor quality, at least the copy is a rather poor quality. utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes, as you know the strongest opinion is with probability bordering on certainty, the next conclusion is highly probable, and the next conclusion below that is probable. So the lower the conclusion, the less information we have to come to this conclusion of identity or not.

utterances.text: I will now move to your conclusions and ask you specific questions for each signature as examined by you, as also shown on page 6 out of 10 of your report to P264 with the ERN number 03523857. And that ERN number is the number of the page. What was your final conclusion, Doctorandus Fagel, as an expert regarding document -- signature Q1?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: The conclusion was that it was highly probable that this questioned signature was written by the author of the reference signatures, Q1 to Q35.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And what was your final conclusion regarding signature on Q2?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: The same conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Signature Q3?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Same conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Signature Q4?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: I could only conclude that this signature was possibly written by the author of the questioned -- reference signatures K1 to K35.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And what was your professional opinion about the questioned signature Q5 in your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: That signature was high probability written by the author of the reference signatures K1 to K35.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And Q6?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Q6, I could give -- Q6, I could give no opinion on this signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And why could you give no opinion?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Because in the first place it's a very poor copy and in the second place it has a different design from the other signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Was there a sign of forgery or can you comment on copying or tracing in regard to this signature?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: As far as I could observe, but that was not too much, there were no signs of copying or tracing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And may I have your final conclusion regarding questioned signature Q7.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Q7, for this signature I came to the conclusion that it's possibly written by the author of the reference signatures.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: For this I came to the conclusion that it was highly probable that this signature was written by the author of the reference signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Q9, the signature questioned.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Also for this signature I came to the conclusion that this was highly probably written by the author of the reference signatures.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: For Q10 I came to the conclusion that this was possibly written by the author of the reference signatures.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: For Q11 I came to the conclusion that this signature was probably written by the author of the reference signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Q12 signature.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: For signature Q12 I came to the conclusion that this was highly probably written by the author of the reference signatures.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Same as for the previous signature.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Same as for the previous signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You mean that both of them are highly probable?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And Q15.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Also for this signature I came to the conclusion that it was highly probably written by the author of the reference samples -- signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Following Q16 signature.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: For signatures Q16, I came to the conclusion that this was -- this one was possibly written by the author of the reference signatures.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: For Q17, I came to the conclusion that this one was highly probably written by the author of the reference samples.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: This signature I came to the conclusion this was highly probably written by the author of the reference signatures.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: This signature I came to the conclusion that it was highly probably written by the author of the reference signatures.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Also for this signature I came to the conclusion that this was highly probably written by the author of the reference signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What was your overall opinion of the probability that the same author -- the same signature applied here with comparison to the known documents and their signatures?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: I don't quite understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I sympathise with you. I suppose you could put the question again because I don't understand it either. It's too vague, actually. I mean, what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I withdraw the question, Your Honour. I finalise now this report. Is there anything you want to add to what you said and clarify it, confirmed to the Judges with regard to this report as an expert?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUS PETRUS FRANCISCUS FAGEL
utterances.text: Well, maybe as I wrote in my report also that it's important to note that the opinions concerning non-original signatures, reproductions, are expressed on the assumption that the non-originals examined are true and accurate representation of the original documents. And furthermore I expect that if the original documents were available for examination, this might result in stronger opinions for the signatures involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this finalised the first report. I would like to move on now to the additional report, that's report E265, report of the 19th of July, 2004, ERN number 03594710 up to 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we start now? We've got four minutes left. It's up to you. If you want the witness to introduce this report while we have an additional report, he can cover this in four minutes or five minutes, we can do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: He can't cover this in the four minutes or five minutes, Your Honour. So I will leave the subsequent order up to this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I do appreciate that today we lost an amount of time dealing with other procedural matters, problems that arose. We have the second report now. How long do you anticipate to be dealing with that -- have this witness deal with this second report?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That should be limited compared to this morning, because this morning we started with the processing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I would imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So in my estimation one hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hour and a half. And then, Mr. Nichols or Madam Vidovic, take it that we will devote the first session of tomorrow's sitting to finish with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour -- I must remind Your Honour of a Mr. Nichols because you -- that's the second time you actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We will need two or three hours, I imagine. Probably a bit more on the side of two hours. It should be short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Should we risk bringing over the other expert tomorrow? Ms. -- Doctorandus Koeijer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if you have the first session and Mr. Jones has two to three hours, that takes us beyond the sitting of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's true. Or perhaps some -- yeah, some ten minutes or half an hour and that's not really productive when it comes to bringing over a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Dr. Koeijer has to come from where? From Rijswijk?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I don't know where he lives, but he has his office in Rijswijk. I also know, happen to know that the office will be removed, so they are in the process of removal as well, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if it is practical to ask him to come for the last session, the last three-quarters of an hour, but not before that. Otherwise, we'll leave him for the day after. But only -- I want to show courtesy to the gentleman and not have him come from wherever in the Netherlands, I don't know where he resides, only to find out that he's still got to go back and come the day after.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, when I look at the time, perhaps it's more productive if he will be called not tomorrow but on Wednesday morning to start. And it's also for him just a fresh start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps the only other thing you can check is whether he by any chance will be here in The Hague, because if he is here in The Hague in any case tomorrow, he could accept to remain -- stand-by wherever he will be and if necessary he will come over. But that's only if he is in The Hague. If he is not in The Hague there's no point in bringing him over and then telling him, very sorry, Doctorandus. Koeijer, please go again and come tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We will inform him is he is available from 1.00, then that will be a good opportunity, if not in The Hague, then he start right away on Wednesday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, for the second report, please Mr. Wubben, your case manager, and our registrar, please make sure that we don't have -- we don't take out the same problems tomorrow. Make sure that all the documents are available, marked, and identified beforehand so that when we start we know exactly where to find them and which documents we are referring to. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just one matter. Just for the record, our case manager is Ms. Jasmina Cosic, our CaseMap manager is Mr. Roberts. This morning when the Prosecution was speaking of sending e-mails to our case manager, I naturally conferred with our case manager, Mr. Roberts is our CaseMap manager. That might explain some of the confusion. In any event, I thought's important to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thanks a lot. I thank you for your cooperation once more. And we will resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning in this same courtroom. Doctorandus Fagel, I thank you very much. You have been extremely helpful. Unfortunately, you need to come back tomorrow. Tomorrow we will try to start on time if there are no problems like we encountered today. I also thank the interpreters, the machine operators and the technicians, and the rest of the staff. Thank you.
